Date: 2026-11-05

Society & Human Rights
• Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong received a 10-year sentence under the national security law, deepening concerns over civil liberties.
• French unions led nationwide strikes for higher wages and reforms as hundreds of thousands took to the streets.
• New Yorkers marched for justice after a Ghanaian teen’s killing; in the UK, debates intensified over sentencing and radical police reform proposals.
• The UK is accused of hardening asylum settlement rules, while research warns flexible academic work may entrench gendered parenting roles.
Why it matters: Protest movements, sentencing debates, and policy shifts are redefining rights, justice, and social norms across democracies.

Geopolitics & Diplomacy
• Democrats regained control of Congress and plan extensive oversight of the Trump administration; several races remain outstanding.
• VP JD Vance blamed the Iran war for GOP losses as conservative media distanced from Trump post-defeat.
• Markets see a Democratic sweep as a moderating force; Europe’s far right recalibrates amid Trump’s setback.
• AI-focused PACs spent heavily with mixed results; OpenAI is courting influence ahead of 2028 with a proposed social contract.
Why it matters: US power shifts will ripple through foreign policy, markets, and transatlantic politics, while tech’s political influence faces reality checks.

Sports

Why it matters: Icons exiting, new sports rising, and leadership contests are reshaping global sport’s competitive and governance dynamics.

Entertainment

Art & Culture
• Pope Leo hosted Bob Dylan at his residence in Rome, reinforcing cultural engagement by the Holy See.
• A Spanish cave revealed spectacular 19,000-year-old engravings; a Dawkins anniversary edition again featured a reversed DNA helix on its cover.
Why it matters: Heritage discoveries and cultural encounters underscore enduring intersections between history, science, and contemporary iconography.

Health & Pandemic
• A US-funded infant vaccine trial in Guinea-Bissau was canceled amid ethical and “neocolonial” concerns about placebo design.
• Six died in a Brooklyn house fire; a lithium-ion battery was found, renewing scrutiny of home battery safety.
• An electricity-emitting toothbrush reduced plaque and gum inflammation in early testing; teens reportedly use cancer drugs to increase height despite risks.
Why it matters: Ethical standards, product safety, and emerging health behaviors demand careful oversight and evidence-based guidance.

Climate & Environment
• Low-producing US oil and gas wells cause 40% of methane emissions despite just 5% of output, study finds.
• Voters pushed back on AI data centers over water and power use; measuring cooling water consumption remains complex.
• Brazil released deforestation and fossil fuel transition roadmaps ahead of COP30; COP31 preview highlights electrification and finance.
• Regulatory rollbacks on carcinogen protections and UK drought, warming seas, and urban greening efforts show mixed governance signals.
Why it matters: Emissions control, resource use, and climate finance decisions will shape resilience and environmental health for decades.

Armed Conflict & Security
• Indonesia rushed thousands of troops to Jakarta amid an alleged presidential wiretap scandal.
• Bodycam footage captured civilians sheltering before a deadly Russian strike in Ukraine; Gaza reported new casualties despite a “ceasefire.”
• Yemen’s government sacked political and military leaders after Houthi gains; multiple European flights received bomb threats; researchers detailed Kremlin-linked mobile exploits.
Why it matters: Political crises, active conflicts, and cyber threats heighten instability and civilian risk across regions.

Other

Why it matters: Wildlife enforcement and practical travel choices shape both conservation outcomes and consumer experiences.

Economy & Markets
• The Bank of England raised rates to 4% amid a cost-of-living squeeze; further hikes are possible absent Middle East conflict resolution.
• A permitting reform bill could accelerate US energy infrastructure; markets cooled after a post-midterm rally as Musk-linked stocks faced pressure.
• AI data center capacity faces political headwinds; AMD’s data center business doubled while gaming slumped; Nintendo sales fell amid memory crunch and supplier exit.
• Amazon teamed with Uber Eats for Prime delivery perks; US jobless claims fell and labor productivity rose.
Why it matters: Policy and market shifts are reshaping investment, corporate strategy, and household finances.

Artificial Intelligence
• Texas’s AI data center boom faces political reversals; nationwide votes signaled resistance to rapid AI infrastructure expansion.
• Big Tech continues record AI spending despite unclear returns; Apple reportedly cut internal AI budgets.
• OpenAI proposed a community compact and policy blueprint to involve locals, increase transparency, and protect ratepayers in data center projects.
• ChatGPT now generates GIFs; Uber saw negligible AI agent bookings; Box adopted Nvidia’s Nemotron to speed agent-first content retrieval.
Why it matters: Public consent, infrastructure policy, and proven utility will determine AI’s pace and shape of deployment.

Longevity & Anti-Aging
• Hormone replacement therapy shows complex, patient-specific relationships with aging clocks in new analyses.
• Senescent cells promote further cellular senescence via extracellular vesicles, exacerbating age-related damage.
Why it matters: Understanding aging mechanisms is key to developing interventions that extend healthy lifespan.
Sources: https://www.fightaging.org/archives/2026/11/hormone-replacement-therapy-exhibits-a-complex-relationship-with-aging-clocks/ | https://www.fightaging.org/archives/2026/11/senescent-cells-promote-senescence-in-other-cells-in-part-via-small-extracellular-vesicle-secretion/

Science & Technology
• NASA unveiled the X-70 Fractal experimental aircraft to test advanced flight controls; Artemis plans aim for a 2028 Moon landing.
• SpaceX partnered with Qualcomm to build a Starlink mobile 5G network; United added a native Spotify app to seatbacks powered by Starlink.
• Agility Robotics debuted on Nasdaq as the first pure-play humanoid robot firm, inviting scrutiny of market readiness.
• Hubble highlighted dwarf galaxy mysteries; China laid out a crewed Moon landing roadmap before 2030.
Why it matters: Advances in aerospace, connectivity, and robotics mark an accelerating technology cycle and intensifying global competition.

Entertainment.title: HOKA x Marni Reunite to Rework the Clifton 11 in Three Bold Colorways
Entertainment.text: Name: Marni x HOKA Clifton 11MSRP: $275 USDRelease Date: November 12Where to Buy: HOKAHOKA and Marni have reunited for a second collaboration, this time reworking the Clifton 11, HOKA’s everyday trainer, as the Clifton Marni. The Clifton’s running credentials stay intact: an engineered mesh upper sits on a compression-molded EVA foam midsole, with HOKA’s Smooth MetaRocker geometry for rolling transitions and a rearfoot-focused Active Foot Frame that supports the heel.MARNI’s influence shows in how those functional parts are treated. Raised 3D silicone lines sweep in waves from the midfoot toward the heel, and the plush collar is lined with a textured knit that contrasts with the smooth mesh.Each of the three colorways takes a different approach to contrast. The Black version is almost completely tonal, from the mesh down to the midsole, with a cream collar lining and red lace loops adding warmth. The Orange pair is the loudest of the three: a vivid orange upper sits on a white midsole wrapped in a metallic silver band, with a black rubber outsole under the forefoot. The White colorway is soft and clean, with a sparkling silver trim along the heel collar.Branding is split across the heel on all three, with a red HOKA logo on the lateral side and Marni’s widely spaced red wordmark on the medial side. Metal lace dubraes add a hardware accent near the toe, and a custom plaid sockliner is tucked inside. MARNI’s eye for pattern carries over to the laces, which come in speckled, striped two-tone designs: black and white on the Orange pair, red and grey on the Black, and pink and grey on the White. Each pair comes with two extra sets of laces for personalizing the look.The Clifton MARNI is set to launch on November 12, 2026, through MARNI's channels, with a wider release following at HOKA and select global retailers on November 13.Set your reminders and get ahead of what’s dropping next on Hypebeast Drops.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: Maya Hawke Draws the Lead Role in Live-Action ‘Magic: The Gathering’ Movie
Entertainment.text: SummaryMaya Hawke has been cast in 'Magic: The Gathering,' a live-action film adaptation of the trading card gameHer role and the plot remain undisclosed, though Hawke is expected to lead an ensemble cast that has yet to be announcedDirector Matt Johnson, a longtime 'Magic' fan, is writing the script with Noah Gardner and Aidan FitzgeraldMaya Hawke is set to star in Magic: The Gathering, Legendary Entertainment and Hasbro Entertainment’s live-action take on the long-running trading card game. Deadline first reported the casting, which puts the Stranger Things actor at the center of one of Hasbro’s biggest properties as it moves to the big screen.Details beyond Hawke’s casting are still limited. Her character has not been revealed, and neither has the storyline, though Deadline reports she is expected to anchor an ensemble that has not yet been cast. That leaves the game’s own lore as the clearest guide to what the film might look like.That lore gives the production a lot to work with. Magic: The Gathering takes place across a multiverse of fantasy worlds, with players battling one another as powerful wizards known as Planeswalkers. Translating that into live action means building several distinct settings instead of a single fantasy realm, which may explain why the cast is being built around a lead before the rest of the ensemble.The team behind the camera brings indie credentials to the franchise. Matt Johnson, the director of Blackberry and creator of Nirvanna the Band the Show, is directing and co-writing the screenplay with Noah Gardner of Super 8 and Aidan Fitzgerald of Calls. Legendary and Hasbro are producing the film together.Johnson’s connection to the game goes well beyond the job. He recalled sitting near the top of the standings going into day two of a Magic Grand Prix in Detroit and seriously considering leaving film school to play professionally, only to lose his composure, make a costly misplay and drive home to Toronto convinced his competitive career was over. “To all the dreamers reading this: in every pool, there is a day 2 deck,” Johnson said.Hawke arrives with a broad résumé across genres. Best known for Netflix’s Stranger Things, she has also appeared in Quentin Tarantino’s Once Upon a Time in Hollywood, Wes Anderson’s Asteroid City, Jennifer Kaytin Robinson’s Do Revenge and Bradley Cooper’s Maestro, and she voiced Anxiety in Pixar’s Inside Out 2. Her next project is Lionsgate’s The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: Santa Monica Studio Delays 'God of War Laufey' to May 2027
Entertainment.text: SummarySanta Monica Studio has pushed the release of God of War Laufey to May 20, 2027The PlayStation 5 exclusive shifts away from its original February 16 launch dateFaye's afterlife narrative will run parallel to the events of the previous two franchise installmentsPlayStation fans will have to wait just a little longer to dive back into the mythological realms, as Santa Monica Studio has officially delayed the release of God of War Laufey. Originally locked in for a February 16, 2027 launch, the highly anticipated PlayStation 5 exclusive has been pushed back by three months and will now officially hit consoles on May 20, 2027. The development team formally announced the schedule change via a social media post, resetting the countdown for a project that was officially revealed this past June.Addressing the shifting timeline, Santa Monica Studio stated that the team is utilizing the extra runway to add essential finishing touches and push the game to its absolute fullest potential. The developer explicitly noted that it does not take fan trust for granted. Moving away from a crowded early 2027 release window provides God of War Laufey with vital breathing room while ensuring Sony secures a major first-party title to anchor its spring quarter.When the game finally drops in May, it promises to flip the established franchise perspective by putting players in control of a brand-new playable protagonist: Faye. Her death in the game's timeline occurs just before the beginning of the 2018 God of War story, serving as the underlying catalyst for the modern saga. Now, players will experience her isolated aftermath. Faye’s story unfolds entirely within the afterlife, focusing heavily on her journey through a mysterious area known as the Everywhen.Because the narrative places her afterlife traversal in this specific setting, God of War Laufey runs completely parallel to the events of both God of War (2018) and God of War Ragnarök. While the fanbase knows the profound impact her passing had on the overarching universe, this upcoming release finally sheds light on her own unseen battles. Alongside the heavy mythological storytelling the studio is known for, the title will also feature some unexpectedly bizarre additions to the lore, including a character described as a talking jelly cube.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: Liverpool Owner Fenway Sports Group Is Reportedly in Talks to Buy a Majority Stake in the Cadillac F1 Team
Entertainment.text: SummaryFenway Sports Group is negotiating a potential £2bn-plus takeover of the Cadillac Formula One teamThe move follows FSG's partial sale of Liverpool to a consortium including Jeff BezosCadillac co-owner Mark Walter is currently offloading sporting assets amid US federal investigationsFenway Sports Group (FSG) is reportedly in talks to acquire a majority stake in the Cadillac Formula One team, a blockbuster move that would command a price tag of more than £2bn. The high-stakes acquisition targets a franchise that only entered the grid this year as a joint venture between General Motors and Mark Walter’s TWG Global. While TWG has firmly denied that any sale of the racing outfit is imminent, FSG stands as just one of several heavy-hitting interested parties currently holding discussions about taking over the team. Representatives for FSG have declined to comment on their investment plans. The potential acquisition signals a massive shift in global sports equity, driven by F1’s remarkable commercial growth across the United States over the last decade. Since the racing series was bought by Liberty Media in 2017, the sport's annual revenue has more than doubled to $4 billion USD.The framework for this multi-billion-pound transaction stems directly from a broader liquidation of assets by Mark Walter. Walter is actively shedding major sports properties amid allegations of insurance fraud, and is currently under investigation by the US Department of Justice and the Securities and Exchange Commission over alleged fraud involving the management of funds at Delaware Life, Clear Spring and EquiTrust. TWG has stated unequivocally that there has been no fraud, yet the firm continues to rapidly reshape its portfolio. The conglomerate already sold off its controlling interest in the Los Angeles Lakers and a 13% stake in Chelsea this past summer, and is currently looking to sell the WNBA’s Los Angeles Sparks. Walter, who remains the controlling owner of the Los Angeles Dodgers, insists that the MLB franchise will not be sold. Sportico previously reported that Walter values his specific shareholding in the Cadillac team at approximately £2.24 billion GBP, though the exact sizes of TWG’s and General Motors' respective stakes have never been made public.Financing a £2 billion GBP F1 entry leverages strategic liquidity generated from FSG's other heavyweight properties. The Boston-based conglomerate recently cashed in on Liverpool, selling a 38% stake this summer to a powerhouse consortium featuring Jeff Bezos and Eduardo Saverin. That partial sale rocketed the Premier League club’s valuation to a staggering £5.5bn, presenting FSG with a monumental profit after they originally paid just £300m for the club in 2010. The consortium that purchased the stake has also secured an option to complete a full takeover of Liverpool before August 2027. FSG’s current sporting investments already span multiple disciplines, including majority stakes in the Boston Red Sox and the Pittsburgh Penguins, alongside a proven history in motorsport through a 50% stake in the Nascar team RFK Racing.Despite the immense financial valuation attached to the Cadillac F1 team, the racing outfit has endured a brutal initiation on the track. The team currently sits at the absolute bottom of the constructors’ championship in their debut season and has yet to win a single point. If successful, buying out a struggling constructor from a motivated seller fundamentally reorients FSG's empire toward F1's soaring American market, swapping legacy European football equity to capitalize on a domestic racing brand.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: ‘GTA VI’ Has Reportedly Pulled In $751 Million USD From Pre-Orders Alone
Entertainment.text: SummaryRockstar’s 'GTA VI' has reportedly generated more than $750 million USD in digital pre-orders weeks before launchAnalytics firm Sensor Tower estimates PS5 players account for 74% of pre-orders, far ahead of Xbox Series X|SThe estimate is already closing in on GTA V’s record first-day sales, though the two figures aren’t a direct comparisonRockstar’s Grand Theft Auto VI is reportedly tracking toward one of the biggest launches in gaming history before a single copy has been unlocked. New estimates from analytics firm Sensor Tower suggest the sequel has already brought in roughly $751 million USD from digital pre-orders across PS5 and Xbox Series X|S, with launch still weeks away.Sensor Tower’s tracking puts the game at around 7.71 million digital pre-orders so far. Momentum appears to be building as release approaches, as the firm estimates that more than $100 million USD of that pre-order revenue came in during the past two weeks alone.The platform split heavily favors Sony. By Sensor Tower’s count, PlayStation accounts for 74% of pre-orders, or roughly 5.74 million copies worth an estimated $559 million USD. Xbox Series X|S makes up the remaining 26%, with about 1.97 million copies bringing in an estimated $192 million USD.The natural benchmark is GTA V, which set a record when it launched in September 2013. Take-Two Interactive’s official figures showed the game passing $800 million USD in worldwide sales within its first 24 hours and crossing $1 billion USD in three days. On paper, GTA VI’s pre-order haul is already approaching that first-day mark before launch day has even arrived.The comparison has limits, though, and the caveats matter. Sensor Tower’s numbers are third-party estimates, not sales data confirmed by Rockstar or Take-Two. They also count only digital pre-orders, so physical copies, often a large share of a blockbuster launch, aren’t included. GTA V’s record, by contrast, reflected actual sales after release, which makes the two figures different kinds of measurement.GTA VI launches November 19 on PS5 and Xbox Series X|S, with preloading set to open on November 10.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: Columbia and BEAMS Flip the 1986 Bugaboo Jacket Inside Out
Entertainment.text: SummaryColumbia and BEAMS rework the 1986 Bugaboo Jacket, replacing its original layered system with a lighter reversible buildA Graphic Sweat Crew with period-style hunting artwork joins the jacket in two gray colorwaysFleece caps in camo and brown round out a compact three-piece capsuleColumbia and BEAMS have reworked the Columbia Bugaboo Jacket for their latest collaboration, turning the 1986 outerwear staple into a reversible piece. The jacket leads a compact capsule that also includes a graphic crewneck and two fleece caps, all styled around the look of the era while being built for everyday wear today.The original Bugaboo became one of the Portland, Oregon outdoor brand’s defining pieces because of its interchange system, which paired a separate inner layer with an outer shell that could be worn together or apart. The collaboration keeps the thinking behind that design but drops the two-piece setup for a reversible construction. As a result, the jacket gives the wearer two looks in a single garment, and BEAMS says the new version is lighter and easier to throw on than the multi-layer original.The jacket comes in brown in sizes S through XL, keeping the palette in the earthy register of classic outdoor gear. The reversible build keeps its versatility while removing the bulk of a zip-in liner, making it better suited to city days than backcountry trips.The Graphic Sweat Crew carries a hunting-themed graphic designed to evoke the period when the Bugaboo first appeared. It comes in gray heather and gray in sizes XS through XL, giving the capsule a lighter layering piece to wear under the jacket.The Fleece Cap finishes the lineup in two one-size colorways. The camo version adds a field-ready pattern, while the brown version matches the jacket and pulls the set together as a coordinated look.Pre-orders for the Columbia x BEAMS collection are open now, ahead of a November 21 release at BEAMS and BEAMS BOY stores (some locations excluded) and the BEAMS online shop. The size S Bugaboo Jacket, the size XS Graphic Sweat Crew and the brown Fleece Cap are available only at BEAMS BOY stores.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: The Moomins Have Moved Into Bottega Veneta’s Intrecciato
Entertainment.text: SummaryBottega Veneta teams up with Moomin on a collection of bags, wallets, charms and home objects based on Tove Jansson’s characters and storiesKey pieces turn story details into leather, from Moominmamma’s striped apron to the walls and roof of MoominhouseThree-dimensional character charms and a hand-crocheted Snufkin figurine extend the house’s leatherwork beyond bagsBottega Veneta has partnered with Moomin on a collection that turns Tove Jansson’s characters, color palettes and storybook scenes into handbags, small leather goods and objects for the home. Rather than putting characters on the surface, the collection builds the references into weaves, hardware and hand-shaped leather, so many of the nods only show up up close.The clearest example is the Small Andiamo, whose design starts from Moominmamma’s striped apron. Red and soft white leathers alternate through the house’s intrecciato weave, and a gold-tone knot detail serves as the hardware. Because the reference comes through in color, the bag works even for someone who has never read the books.Several other silhouettes hide their story references in less obvious places. The Large Pinacoteca tote carries comic strip panels, and select wallets use blue and red tones that echo the exterior walls and roof of Moominhouse. On the Small Cabat, the original cover art from Comet in Moominland is placed on the internal pouch, so the reference is only visible once the bag is open.The leather charms are where the craft becomes most sculptural. Artisans hand-weave the Moomintroll charm from tubular Nappa leather to recreate his round shape, while the Moominmamma charm adds her striped apron and a miniature intrecciato bag of her own. A Moominhouse charm and a pencil holder stocked with colored pencils carry the story’s architecture into everyday objects.The Snufkin figurine is the most labor-intensive piece in the collection. It is made from finely cut Nappa leather worked with a crochet technique that takes artisans several days to finish. The result has a tactile, three-dimensional texture that differs from the house’s usual woven bags, showing how far the collaboration stretches Bottega Veneta’s leather techniques.The Bottega Veneta x Moomin collection launches early in Japan at an Isetan Shinjuku pop-up on November 11. It then rolls out on November 18 to the Ginza and Omotesando flagships, the Hankyu Umeda leather goods store and Bottega Veneta’s Japanese website.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Art & Culture.title: Sit on It or Stack It: Carpet Company’s S-Tool Can Do Both
Art & Culture.text: SummaryCarpet Company’s S-Tool reimagines the humble screw as a stackable fiberglass stool designed in Baltimore.Each 12-inch piece weighs nearly 20 pounds and carries its own individually numbered plaque.Batch 2 introduces Navy, Clementine, Rose, Slime and Jet Black colorways.Baltimore's Carpet Company is carrying its design language past skateboarding and apparel with the S-Tool, a fiberglass stool built from scratch that blurs the line between furniture and sculpture. The concept takes its cue from humble hardware: each of its four chunky legs tapers into the fluted point of a screw, while the seat's surface is stamped with four Phillips-head recesses, turning an everyday fastener into a playful, oversized object.Carpet Company leans fully into that irreverence, pitching the piece with the tagline "Sit on it. Stand on it. Spit on it." and suggesting it can serve as anything from a chair, ottoman or footrest to a paperweight, chew toy or even trash, depending on how its owner chooses to use it.Despite measuring just 12 inches tall, the S-Tool carries real heft at close to 20 pounds, giving its compact frame a grounded, substantial presence. Its high-gloss finish amplifies the toy-like silhouette, and the design does more than look good: the screw-tip legs nest into the recesses of the stool below, allowing multiple units to stack into a seamless, totem-like column.Flip one over and a metal plaque on the underside lists its colorway and individual number, with the Batch 2 plaques shown in the imagery reading "of 7." The presentation extends to the packaging, a white cube printed with rows of multicolored screws, the brand's tongue-in-cheek usage notes and a grinning blue hippo graphic on a red panel, along with a leather-bound book that showcases each shade as an illustrated screw.The S-Tool's first run arrived in Red, Yellow, Kelly, Blue and Chocolate and sold out almost immediately. For Batch 2, Carpet Company introduced five new colorways: Navy, Clementine, Rose, Slime and Jet Black. Like the debut collection, quantities are extremely limited, reinforcing the S-Tool's status as both a usable piece of furniture and a collectible design object. For more information, head over to the brand's website.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Climate & Environment.title: ‘It’s kind of a melting pot’: how one US city transformed a highway into a leafy oasis
Climate & Environment.text:
The BLVD is home to 250 enterprises, from banks, tattoo shops and restaurants to museums and a performing arts centrePassing through the Mojave desert on State Route 14, going by landscapes Hollywood uses to represent alien planets, a driver might not expect to find a walkable, tree-lined boulevard.
 
 
 But there are nine beautiful, leafy blocks on West Lancaster Boulevard, a piece of what used to be Highway 14. They were redeveloped as part of a mixed-use urban streetscape in the city of Lancaster, California in 2010.
 
 
 The BLVD, as it’s been rebranded, is home to 250 public and private enterprises, from banks, tattoo shops and restaurants to museums, a performing arts centre and a public library. City Hall is just a block south.
 
 
 The city invested $11.5m (£8.5m) to transform a busy thoroughfare into an inviting public space. The three lanes in the centre of the former five-lane road were replaced by a series of tree-lined ramblas – Spanish for “avenue” and “watercourse,” because dry stream beds served as streets in early cities.The redesign was planned and funded by the city of redevelopment agency. Within four years of completion, it had generated more than $270m in economic output, attracted $130m in investment, created hundreds of jobs and prompted the building or renovation of hundreds of housing units, according to the city.
 
 
 The revitalisation has also created more intangible benefits, residents say.. The city centre the feels like a gathering space, they said — somewhere where they can feel like part of a community. Continue reading...

Science & Technology.title: Why a Mathematician Is Chasing Eclipses With Algorithms and Cameras
Science & Technology.text: The sun hangs low over the plains of Castile and León, in the north-central region of Spain. But from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza, it appears that a few puffy white clouds have started to block the sun. That’s vexing.A group of researchers, some wearing cardboard eclipse glasses, is clustered around sets of portable telescopes and cameras connected to laptops. All this gear is scattered on tabletops perched on the mountainside. On the computer screens, the sun’s disk looks like a deep orange crescent that is slowly waning. That’s because the moon began to crawl across it about half an hour ago. In 25 minutes, it will obscure the sun completely, producing an eerie and wondrous phenomenon—a total solar eclipse.In the late-summer, late-afternoon heat, the researchers watch anxiously as those fluffy clouds linger around the sun. From an abandoned hut on the slope a few meters above, where the researchers have set up camp, one of the grad students emerges and nods toward the cloud formation. “Do you think it will dissolve?” he blurts out.“It will.” Miloslav Druckmüller glances calmly at his group of doctoral candidates, now making final checks of the equipment in preparation for totality. Here in Spain, on this 12th day of August, Druckmüller is getting ready for his 19th solar eclipse. He knows from long experience that weather can turn quickly when the moon’s shadow suddenly pushes the temperature down. Plus, there’s no sense in riling up the grad students any more than they already are. Miloslav Druckmüller led the design and construction of a unique optical instrument that incorporates eight astrocameras. Each is equipped with a spectral filter for sensing and recording specific emission spectra from the solar corona. Each of those spectra, in turn, is associated with a particular ionic species of iron atoms. Because the temperature needed to ionize iron varies depending on the ionic species, analyzing the locations and relative abundance of these ionic species offers valuable insights into the distribution of heat in the corona.Václav ŠirokýDuring totality, the moon blocks the overwhelming glare of the solar disk, revealing delicate structures in the sun’s outer atmosphere, the corona. Using custom-built telescope systems and image-processing techniques that Druckmüller has spent decades developing, the researchers aim to gain insights into the processes in this enigmatic region that is otherwise hard to study. In addition to imaging the visible coronal light, the team will try to track the dispersal of superhot ions of iron into interplanetary space, which could give rare insights into the pattern of heat emanating from the corona.And they’ll have 107 seconds to do all that.A Mathematician’s Path to Solar Eclipse PhotographyDruckmüller is a professor of mathematics and image processing at the Brno University of Technology in the Czech Republic and a leading figure in the Solar Wind Sherpas, an international team that studies the sun’s corona during total eclipses. In the solar eclipse world, he is nothing short of a legend, albeit a reluctant one.An image from Miloslav Druckmüller’s first solar-eclipse expedition, to Hungary, vividly shows Baily’s Beads. These elongated white lights along a piece of the left edge of the blacked-out solar disk are caused by beams of sunlight shining through gaps in the irregular lunar surface during the eclipse. The pink shapes are solar prominences, which are jets of plasma extending out into space and held in place by the sun’s intense magnetic field.Miloslav DruckmüllerHe photographed his first solar eclipse in 1999, in what he thought would be a one-off lark. During that eclipse, the moon’s deep shadow missed Druckmüller’s native Czechia by just a few tens of kilometers, so he chased it to Hungary with a 30-year-old Soviet MTO 1,000-millimeter lens. All he remembers from that day is the rush of adrenaline he felt while trying to find the sun in the sky with the lens’s minuscule field of view and keep it in focus for the two minutes of the eclipse.He insists that he has never enjoyed any of the eclipses he has photographed. “In fact, I have never properly seen any of those eclipses. You are just watching the screens, making sure that it’s all doing what it’s supposed to do. There are so many things that can go wrong and you can’t redo it.”A composite sequence of photographs shows the 12 August 2026 solar eclipse as seen from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain.Václav Široký and Miloslav DruckmüllerDespite Druckmüller’s outward tranquility on this Spanish hillside, the stakes are high. Just 45 minutes ago, his group heard from their colleagues in Iceland, where viewing conditions had promised to be better than in Spain. But a vast low-pressure system had clouded the entire sky, leaving all three Iceland teams without a view.What Solar Eclipses Reveal About the CoronaThe corona has been a mystery for centuries. Though dimmer—by a factor of a million—than the sun’s visible surface, the corona is nevertheless extremely hot: about a million degrees Celsius compared to 5,500 degrees on the surface. Because the sun’s nuclear fusion engine churns at the star’s heart, it might seem that temperatures should fall farther from the core.To observe the faint corona in visible light, researchers must block the sun’s ferocious glare. Specialized telescopes called coronagraphs do this with an opaque disk called an occulter. But because light bends around the occulter’s edges in an effect called diffraction, it must block an area much larger than that of the solar disk to prevent light from spilling over and ruining the images. But doing so means obstructing the inner part of the corona, which harbors the most important processes that underpin the puzzling phenomena of the sun’s upper atmosphere.That’s why total eclipses matter so much to solar physicists. By sheer chance, the moon is exactly the right size and at just the right distance to completely cover the sun during a total solar eclipse. Because the moon is so far away from Earth, the view is not marred by diffraction, and the corona reveals itself nearly all the way down to the sun’s surface.Space probes can image the solar surface in other wavelengths, but those views have limitations, too. Spacecraft such as NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory do see the innermost parts of the corona in extreme ultraviolet light, explains Shadia Habbal, a solar physicist at the University of Hawaii and leader of the Solar Wind Sherpas project. “But it cuts off very quickly, so you don’t see its extension into space as well as we can see it in the visible emission lines” during an eclipse. “That’s the biggest advantage,” she says, of solar eclipse photography.The European Proba-3 mission, launched in 2024, simulates total solar eclipses by flying two spacecraft in a formation 150 meters apart with one acting as an occulter and the other as the telescope. The instruments aboard that satellite, however, have limitations compared to the equipment used by the Solar Wind Sherpas team.How Eclipse Images Sparked a Scientific PartnershipWhen Druckmüller developed the film from his 1999 eclipse expedition, the photographs didn’t do justice to the event’s eerie beauty. He spent countless evenings applying his expertise in numerical image processing in an attempt to re-create in his photographs the sights he witnessed in that Hungarian corn field.It took two years, but eventually he succeeded. Where before there were dull views of the blackened lunar disk surrounded by the blunt wisps of the corona, Druckmüller revealed the subtlest details of the magnetic field lines stretching from the sun far into space. As his photographs circulated among solar physicists, invitations to eclipse expeditions began to arrive.Habbal learned about the images from a Ph.D. student who had seen them at a conference presentation that didn’t credit Druckmüller. When Habbal’s team later published the images in a paper, they misattributed them to another researcher. Druckmüller found out through an astrophysicist friend. “I wrote her a rather disappointed email and she responded within 10 minutes,” Druckmüller recalls. “She really didn’t have a clue.”The error was corrected, and within weeks, Habbal and Druckmüller began a collaboration that grew into a friendship. “Milos’s processing brings out details that nobody has seen before, and they tell you a lot about very tiny features in the corona that you don’t see otherwise,” says Habbal.How Image Processing Reveals the Solar CoronaCapturing the corona’s delicate structures means finding a way to show its brightest and faintest features in the same image. “During the solar eclipse, the contrast between the darkest and brightest parts of the corona is enormous, possibly one to a million,” Druckmüller explains. “But a computer monitor only allows you to display a contrast ratio of one to about 800.” (Some modern monitors, particularly OLED ones, can deliver higher contrast ratios.)The human eye can adjust to this enormous range of brightness, allowing an observer to see both the bright corona and the faint stars and planets that briefly emerge in the darkened sky. To bring those details together in a photograph, Druckmüller uses custom image-processing algorithms to combine exposures that capture different parts of that range.Researchers Martin Šebek and Peter Urgoš make fine adjustments to the focus and alignment of the astrocameras on a key optical instrument before the 12 August solar eclipse.Václav ŠirokýTo create a single image, Druckmüller’s teams need to take 200 individual frames during the eclipse at exposure times ranging from 0.001 second to two seconds. The data must then be calibrated against a vast number of reference images to filter out noise and imperfections. Flat fields, which depict a uniform light background, help correct for defects caused by telescope optics, dust spots, and variations in pixel sensitivity. Dark frames, taken with light blocked from the sensor, help correct for artifacts created by the camera’s image sensor itself. “It takes the computer more than two days to process one image,” Druckmüller says. Including the calibration data, a single finished image requires about 3,000 input frames.Choosing a Location for Solar Eclipse PhotographySince 2008, teams directed by Habbal and Druckmüller have traveled to every total solar eclipse, spreading out across multiple locations to hedge against bad weather. About half of the teams return with usable data. For the others, it’s just a short and stressful voyage. For the 12 August eclipse, three groups deployed to Iceland and two to Spain.The teams seek sites close to the center of the band of totality, where the moon blocks the sun for longest. In Spain, the 12 August band of totality cut across the north of the country; the center line of the shadow passed within 11 kilometers of Pico Trigaza, promising Druckmüller and his colleagues a precious 107 seconds of totality.But duration is only part of the calculation. Totality on Pico Trigaza will commence 51 minutes before sunset, with the sun just 8 degrees above the horizon. That low, the rays must pass through a much thicker layer of the atmosphere than when the sun is higher in the sky, increasing the light distortion that complicates photography. At the researchers’ camp on Pico Trigaza, 1,600 meters above sea level, the thinner air should help a bit.An abandoned hut on the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain was spruced up so that it could serve as a home base for the research team recording the 12 August solar eclipse.Martin Šebek“Iceland would have been a much better place for us than Spain because the sun was higher up, some 25 degrees above the horizon,” Druckmüller says wistfully. But Iceland’s notoriously unpredictable weather made Spain an essential backup. If you pack a van with thousands of dollars’ worth of cameras and optical gear and then set out on a 2,351-kilometer journey, you shouldn’t be surprised if you finish the trip with a few striking photographs [top]. The sleeping arrangements for the grad students at the Pico Trigaza hut [bottom] were spartan, but the views were first-rate.Top: Martin Šebek; Bottom: Václav ŠirokýOn the mountain, locals have spruced up a rustic, long-unused hut for the researchers, running power cables from a nearby telecommunication outpost and bringing in a water tank. Five Ph.D. students drove more than 2,000 kilometers from Brno and have spent nearly a week preparing the equipment. Druckmüller and his wife joined them two days before the eclipse. They cook on a small propane grill and sleep in sleeping bags on yoga mats. “We have plenty of space here to set up our telescopes, beautiful views, and a roof over our heads,” Druckmüller says with a grin. “It’s perfect.”But even the best equipment and a carefully chosen site count for nothing if the clouds roll in. “So much work goes into the preparations and then, if you end up with nothing, you just feel terrible sadness,” says Jana Hoderová, an assistant professor of mathematics at Brno University of Technology and one of Druckmüller’s key collaborators.As the moon continues to slide in front of the solar disk, the pesky cumulus cloud that kept everybody on edge begins to dissolve. It’s 10 minutes to totality. The relief is palpable.Mapping the Solar Corona’s Temperature With Iron The countdown on the computers that control the cameras has begun. The screens are now showing only a tiny orange sliver, and the evening is becoming perceptibly less bright.Twenty astrophotography cameras, most of them drawing power from a car battery that was also buffering the cameras from any grid instabilities, are pointed at the sun. Alongside equipment capturing the corona’s visible light, the team has built an assembly of eight cameras to detect light emitted by various iron ions that arise in the corona. Among the optical gear assembled at Pico Trigaza to capture the 12 August solar eclipse was a unique instrument designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona [at left]. Václav ŠirokýThose instruments looking for iron ions have been put together with resourcefulness and thrift. A colleague of Druckmüller’s laser-cut the aluminum plates holding the carefully aligned lenses in exchange “for two bottles of whisky.” The brackets and attachments were 3D-printed at Brno University of Technology. The lenses, produced for the defunct camera maker Contax, were bought at steep discounts on eBay. By far the most expensive elements are interference filters that isolate the wavelengths emitted by the iron ions.Around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still.“That’s something nobody else in the world can do,” Druckmüller says with visible satisfaction. The unique technology, codeveloped with Habbal’s Hawaii team, has already enabled researchers to map the distribution of temperatures across the entire corona and to discover previously unseen structures, dubbed “smoke rings,” in the coronal plasma. The photographs also revealed the boundary region where the solar plasma becomes so thin that its ions stop colliding. The optical assembly designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona is outfitted with astrocameras, each of which captures spectra from a different ionic species. To do that, each astrocamera is equipped with a spectral filter whose bandwidth is so narrow—one nanometer—that the filter appears as a mirror.Martin Fornůsek“Iron is the most abundant of the heavy elements that we see in the solar corona,” says Habbal. “And because the corona is so hot, the iron atoms lose electrons and get ionized. The larger the loss, the higher the temperature.”For example, a temperature of around 1.6 million °C is necessary to produce an iron ion that has lost 12 electrons. But only 1.4 million °C is needed to strip an iron atom of 11 electrons. Once it’s in a particular electrical state, the ion retains its specific ionization, even as it travels outward with the solar wind. Each of those ions, whether +11 or +12, emits a different wavelength of light, allowing the researchers to map not just temperatures within the corona, but also how those iron ions spread into interplanetary space and distribute heat. Habbal and her colleagues had long been trying to image those iron ions during solar eclipses. But it wasn’t until Druckmüller entered the picture that they were able to develop the gear and the mathematical techniques to do it.Three, Two, One…TotalityWith just a minute to go to totality, the researchers begin removing protective filters from the lenses. It’s 50 minutes to sunset, and the waning sun has just begun to light up the clouds above the horizon with the first tinge of orange. Then, suddenly, the evening begins a rapid and premature descent into darkness. Along the edge of the fantastically thin solar crescent, the brilliant orange points known as Baily’s Beads flash and disappear—the last fragments of photospheric light visible through deep lunar valleys. As totality begins, observers remove their glasses. The hot air cools. The graduate students remain quietly and intently focused on their gear.Druckmüller looks up from his camera toward the darkened plains. Around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still. The sky is ablaze with fiery colors all along the horizon where the deep lunar shadow drops off. Venus burns brilliantly in the southwest, a sharp white pinpoint in the darkened sky. The sound of camera shutters suddenly fills the air. Then, as quickly as it fell, the darkness begins to recede, bid farewell with another handful of golden Baily’s Beads.The crowd erupts in cheers. The Ph.D. students throw themselves at each other and hug like they mean it.“The students did most of the work this time, so I actually allowed myself to really look at it,” Druckmüller says. “It was beautiful. Pico Trigaza may not have been the best for science photography, but from the aesthetic point of view, it was extraordinary.”  The 2026 solar-eclipse team at Pico Trigaza in Spain included [from left] Magdalena Šrotířová, Peter Urgoš, Martin Fornůsek, Miloslav Druckmüller, Václav Široký, and Martin Šebek.Václav ŠirokýBut for Druckmüller, this is just the beginning. While other eclipse chasers will race to release their images, he will take his time. He expects to publish the first visible-light images of the corona in about two weeks. Processing the iron-ion images, and uncovering whatever insights they may hold, will take months—maybe even a whole year.“Probably until the next eclipse in 2027” in North Africa, Druckmüller says.Who knows? Maybe he’ll even enjoy that one, too.

Science & Technology.title: Apple Is Reportedly Working on a Robotic Arm Smart Display for 2028
Science & Technology.text: SummaryApple is actively developing a $1,000 robotic smart display internally codenamed J595The hardware boasts a 9-inch screen on an articulated arm capable of 360-degree rotationSoftware teams are holding the launch for a projected 2028 release to perfect AI integrationApple is currently developing a high-end expansion to its smart home display lineup, with a report from The Information shedding light on an unreleased product featuring a moving robotic arm. Former Apple employees state that the company could ultimately brand this higher-end model as the Apple HomeView Ultra. Internally carrying the codename J595, the robotic display product carries an estimated price tag of around $1,000 USD. Arriving at a $700 USD premium over the $299 USD standard Apple HomeView announced last month, this device expands Apple's connected smart home ecosystem into the high-end market.The defining design element of the upcoming HomeView Ultra is its physical footprint, featuring a 9-inch display that swivels around a robotic arm. This hardware closely resembles a classic articulated desk lamp, bearing a direct similarity to the fixture featured in Pixar's logo. A separate report from MacRumors notes that the 9-inch screen features full 360-degree capabilities. Rather than remaining static on a counter, the robotic display device uses built-in sensors to follow users as they move around a space during FaceTime calls.Despite the futuristic design, physical engineering is complete, as hardware for the HomeView Ultra has been ready for two years. Apple's software team is currently delaying the launch to fine-tune integrated AI and home automation features. Holding the release allows developers to refine complex automated responses before delivering robotic hardware to consumers. One planned automation feature involves the display automatically switching on a light when someone enters the room.Because of this intentional software delay, early adopters must wait several years to purchase the technology. The Information states that Apple could formally announce the device in 2027 and begin shipping to buyers in 2028. This launch timeline aligns with Bloomberg reporting from last month regarding a projected 2027 or 2028 release window.
